module_title: Scalding, Dehairing, and Singeing the Carcass

lessons.title: Heating water to the correct temperature for scalding
lessons.body:
Scalding a pig is the key step that loosens the hair so it can be scraped off easily. The water must be hot enough to work but not so hot that it cooks the skin. The ideal temperature is between 60Â°C and 65Â°C (140Â°F to 149Â°F). If you don't have a thermometer, use the elbow test: dip your elbow into the water. It should feel very hot but not scalding. Another test is to dip a small area of the pig's back for a few seconds; if the hair comes off easily when you rub it, the temperature is right. If the water is too cool, the hair will be hard to remove. If it's too hot, the skin will turn pale and start to cook, making it tough and prone to tearing.  

To heat water, use a large pot or a metal drum over a fire or gas burner. For a whole pig, you'll need 50 to 100 litres of water, depending on the size of the pig. Start with clean water. Bring it to a boil, then let it cool slightly or mix with cold water to reach the right temperature. Stir the water well before testing.  

In many African settings, people use a large drum cut in half or a built-in concrete tank. If you're using a drum, make sure it's clean and free of rust. You can also add a little wood ash to the water; this helps break down the hair and makes scraping easier. But don't add too muchâabout one handful per 20 litres is enough.  

Always have a source of cold water nearby to adjust the temperature if it gets too hot. Keep a thermometer if possible, but learn the feel test. With practice, you'll know by touch. Remember, the goal is to scald, not boil. Work quickly once the pig is in the water, as the temperature will drop. If you're scalding more than one pig, reheat the water between animals.  

Safety note: Never leave the fire unattended, and keep children away from the hot water. Use gloves and long sleeves to protect yourself from splashes.

lessons.title: Immersion and scraping techniques for removing hair
lessons.body:
Once the water is at the right temperature, it's time to immerse the pig. If you have a large enough container, lower the whole pig into the water. If not, you can scald one half at a time. Hold the pig by the legs or use ropes to lower it carefully. Make sure the water covers the area you want to scald. Leave the pig in the water for 2 to 5 minutes. The time depends on the pig's size and hair thickness. For a small pig, 2 minutes may be enough; for a large one, up to 5 minutes.  

After soaking, pull the pig out and place it on a clean surface, like a wooden pallet or a tarp. Immediately begin scraping the hair off with a sharp knife or a specialized scraper. A dull knife will tear the skin, so keep it sharp. Use a pulling motion, not pushing, to avoid cutting the skin. Scrape in the direction of the hair growth. You'll see the hair and a thin layer of dirt come off. Rinse the scraper often in clean water.  

Work quickly because the hair becomes harder to remove as the pig cools. If you're scalding half at a time, do the first half, then flip the pig and scald the other half. For hard-to-reach areas like the head, ears, and between the legs, use a smaller knife or even a spoon to scrape. Be careful around the eyes and snout.  

After scraping, check for any remaining hair. If there are patches, you can re-dip that area in hot water for a few seconds and scrape again. But don't over-scald. Once the hair is mostly off, rinse the pig with clean water to remove loose hair and dirt.  

In many African communities, people work together: one person holds the pig, another scrapes, and a third keeps the water hot. This teamwork makes the job faster. Remember to keep the work area clean and dispose of hair properly to avoid attracting flies.

lessons.title: Using a blowtorch or fire to singe remaining hair
lessons.body:
After scraping, there will still be fine hairs and sometimes stubborn patches. Singeing removes these and also helps to kill bacteria on the skin. You can use a blowtorch, a gas torch, or even a fire made with dry grass or wood. If using a blowtorch, keep the flame at a medium setting and hold it about 15-20 cm away from the skin. Move the flame back and forth quickly so you don't burn the skin. You want to singe the hair, not cook the meat.  

If you don't have a blowtorch, you can use a fire. Build a small fire with dry grass or straw. Once it's burning well, pass the pig over the flames, turning it so all sides get exposed. Be careful not to let the pig catch fire. You can also use a metal sheet to reflect heat onto the pig. Another method is to use a hot iron rod or a piece of metal heated in the fire and run it over the skin.  

Singeing should be done in a well-ventilated area, as the burning hair produces a strong smell and smoke. Wear gloves and keep a bucket of water nearby in case of emergencies. After singeing, the skin will be blackened in spots. That's normal. You'll scrape off the burnt layer in the next step.  

In some African traditions, singeing is done with a blowtorch fueled by kerosene or gas. If you use a blowtorch, check the hose and connections for leaks before lighting. Never point the torch at yourself or others. Keep children away.  

Singeing not only removes hair but also gives the skin a nice golden color and a crispy texture after cooking. It's an important step for a clean, professional finish.

lessons.title: Scraping and washing the skin for a clean finish
lessons.body:
After singeing, the pig's skin will have burnt hair and a black layer. You need to scrape this off to get a clean, white skin. Use a sharp knife or a metal scraper. Work on a clean surface. Scrape firmly but carefully, using short strokes. You'll see the black layer come off, revealing the clean skin underneath. Rinse the scraper often in water.  

For tough spots, you can dip the scraper in water or use a little ash as an abrasive. Ash also helps to remove any remaining hair and neutralizes odors. After scraping, wash the entire pig with clean water. You can use a brush to scrub the skin, especially in crevices like the armpits, groin, and between the toes.  

If you want an extra clean finish, you can wash the pig with a mixture of water and lime juice or vinegar. This helps to remove any lingering smell and brightens the skin. Rinse thoroughly with clean water.  

After washing, dry the pig with a clean cloth or let it air dry. The skin should be smooth and free of hair. Any remaining hair can be removed with a razor or a small knife. Check the skin for any cuts or bruises.  

In many African markets, a clean, well-singed pig fetches a better price. Take your time with this step. A clean carcass is not only more appealing but also safer to eat because dirt and bacteria are removed.  

Finally, inspect the skin for any wounds or abscesses. If you find any, cut them out and discard. Wash your hands and tools thoroughly after handling raw meat.

lessons.title: Removing hooves and lower legs
lessons.body:
Removing the hooves and lower legs is done after the skin is cleaned. You can do this with a sharp knife, a meat saw, or a cleaver. First, locate the joint between the hoof and the leg. It's usually a visible line where the hair changes or where the leg narrows. Place the pig on its back or side.  

If using a knife, make a cut around the leg just above the hoof, cutting through the skin and tendons. Then bend the hoof backward to expose the joint. Cut through the joint with a knife or saw. For larger pigs, a saw is easier. If you have a cleaver, you can chop through the bone with a firm strike.  

After removing the hooves, you may want to remove the lower legs up to the knee or hock. This is optional but often done for easier handling. Cut through the joint at the knee. Again, use a saw or cleaver for the bone.  

In some African cultures, the hooves and lower legs are cleaned and cooked as delicacies, often in soups or stews. If you plan to use them, wash them thoroughly and remove any hair or dirt. You can singe them again if needed.  

If you're not using them, dispose of them properly. Don't leave them lying around, as they can attract flies and rodents.  

Always use a stable cutting surface, like a sturdy table or chopping block. Keep your knives sharp and cut away from your body. Wear gloves if you have them. After removing the hooves, wash the legs with clean water and continue with the next steps of processing.  

Remember, clean cuts make the carcass look better and reduce the risk of contamination.

lessons.title: Inspecting the skin for wounds or abscesses
lessons.body:
Inspecting the skin is a crucial step for food safety. After the pig is scalded, scraped, and singed, look over the entire skin carefully. You're looking for wounds, abscesses, bruises, or any signs of disease. A healthy pig skin should be smooth, pale, and free of lumps or discharges.  

Start at the head and work your way down. Check the ears, eyes, snout, and mouth. Look for cuts, sores, or swelling. Then move to the neck, shoulders, back, and sides. Feel the skin with your hands; you might detect lumps that you can't see. Abscesses are pockets of pus that can be felt as soft or firm lumps under the skin. If you find one, cut it out with a clean knife, making sure to remove all the infected tissue. Discard it properly.  

Also check the belly, groin, and legs. Look for ticks, lice, or other parasites. If you see ticks, remove them with tweezers and dispose of them. Wash the area with disinfectant.  

If you find many abscesses or signs of serious disease, like widespread redness or foul smell, the meat may not be safe to eat. In that case, consult a veterinarian or discard the carcass.  

In African settings, where pigs may be raised in free-range conditions, wounds from fighting or accidents are common. Minor cuts can be trimmed away. But always err on the side of caution.  

After inspection, wash the carcass again with clean water. This step ensures that only healthy meat goes to market or to your family's table. It also protects you and your customers from foodborne illnesses.  

Keep records of any abnormalities you find, as this can help you improve your pig husbandry practices.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Scalding, Dehairing, and Singeing the Carcass

In small and medium pig-processing enterprises across Africa â from backyard slaughter slabs in Uganda to semi-commercial abattoirs in Nigeria and Kenya â the scalding, dehairing, and singeing stage determines both the saleable yield and the market price of the carcass. A clean, evenly white skin with no residual bristles, no scorch marks, and no abscesses can raise the value of a dressed pig by 10â20% compared with a poorly finished carcass. Buyers in butcheries, hotels, and open markets judge quality first by the skin. This lesson gives you the practical numbers, timings, and techniques to get it right every time.

1. Heating Water to the Correct Temperature for Scalding

Scalding loosens the hair follicles and the outer layer of the epidermis so the bristles can be scraped off without tearing the skin. The target water temperature is 60â65 Â°C (140â149 Â°F) for adult pigs. Below 58 Â°C the hair will not release; above 70 Â°C the skin cooks, turns grey, and becomes difficult to scrape â this is called "scalding burn" and it damages the hide permanently.

In field conditions, most processors judge temperature by eye and hand, which is unreliable. A simple thermometer (even a cheap digital kitchen probe) pays for itself within one pig. If no thermometer is available, the traditional test is to dip a finger: at 60â65 Â°C you can hold your hand in the water for 2â3 seconds before it becomes painful. This is a rough guide only â invest in a thermometer.

Table 1: Recommended scalding water temperature and time by pig weight class
Pig weight class Live weight Water temp (Â°C) Immersion time Notes
Piglet / suckling 5â15 kg 58â60 1â2 min Skin is thin; use lower end of range
Weaner / grower 15â50 kg 60â63 2â4 min Most common in smallholder slaughter
Finisher / market hog 50â90 kg 62â65 3â5 min Standard commercial range
Heavy adult / sow 90â150 kg 63â65 4â6 min Thicker skin, coarser bristles
Boar (if used) 100â180 kg 64â66 5â7 min Strong odour; consider separate handling

Source: Adapted from FAO, "Guidelines for slaughtering, meat cutting and further processing" (FAO Animal Production and Health Paper 91, 1991), and from the Uganda National Bureau of Standards, US EAS 12:2013, "Fresh pork â Specification."

Business tip: A 200-litre drum of water heated to 63 Â°C scalds 2â3 pigs before it drops below 58 Â°C. Plan your kill order: scald the heaviest pigs first while the water is hottest, then the lighter ones. Reheat between batches rather than topping up with cold water, which wastes fuel.

2. Immersion and Scraping Techniques for Removing Hair

Immersion must be complete and even. The pig should be fully submerged â including the head, ears, armpits, and the inside of the legs â for the full time. In practice, most African small-scale operations use a half-drum or a purpose-built scalding tank. The pig is held under with a hook or a wooden pole; it should be rolled and turned so that all surfaces contact the hot water.

After immersion, lift the pig onto a scraping table or clean concrete slab. Use a bell scraper (also called a hog scraper) or, if unavailable, a blunt knife, a piece of broken hoe blade, or a metal pot lid. Scrape with the grain of the hair, working from the head towards the tail. Do not press too hard â you want to remove hair and the outer skin layer, not cut into the flesh.

Scrape in sections: head and ears first, then the back and flanks, then the belly and inner thighs, then the legs and feet. Re-dip the pig briefly if the hair starts to set again. A common mistake is to leave the head and ears until last â by then the water has cooled and the hair is difficult to remove. Do the head first.

3. Using a Blowtorch or Fire to Singe Remaining Hair

Even after careful scraping, fine hairs and bristle roots remain, especially on the head, ears, legs, and around the belly. Singeing removes these and also helps to firm the skin and reduce surface bacteria. Two methods are common in Africa:

  • Blowtorch (gas): Fastest and most controllable. Use a standard propane or butane torch. Keep the flame moving constantly â never hold it in one spot. The skin should darken slightly and the hair should curl and burn off, not char the skin. Work from head to tail, then the legs and belly.
  • Open fire (straw, wood, or dried grass): Traditional and cheap. The carcass is passed over a low flame or laid on a clean metal sheet over hot coals. This requires two people: one to turn the carcass, one to control the fire. Avoid smoke from treated or painted wood â it contaminates the meat.

After singeing, scrape the skin again with a blunt scraper or knife to remove burnt hair and the scorched outer layer. This second scrape is what gives the carcass its clean, white appearance. Then wash thoroughly with clean water.

4. Scraping and Washing the Skin for a Clean Finish

The final finish is achieved by scraping, washing, and â in premium markets â a light shave with a sharp knife. Use clean, potable water. If the local water supply is questionable, add a small amount of food-grade sanitiser (e.g., 50â100 ppm chlorine) to the final rinse. This is especially important for pork destined for urban butcheries or export.

Hang the carcass on a rail or gambrel and wash from top to bottom with a hose or a bucket and clean cloth. Pay attention to the armpits, groin, ears, and between the toes. A clean carcass dries to a pale pink-white colour; a poorly washed one looks grey and smells off within hours.

Table 2: Common skin defects, causes, and business impact
Defect Cause Business impact Prevention
Scalding burn (grey, cooked skin) Water above 70 Â°C or too long immersion 10â25% price discount; skin unsaleable as crackling Thermometer; 60â65 Â°C; 3â5 min max
Residual bristles Water too cool; insufficient scraping Buyer rejection; rework cost Check temp; scrape head first; singe
Scorch marks / charring Blowtorch held too long in one spot Cosmetic downgrade Keep flame moving; train operators
Abscesses / wounds Injection sites, fighting, poor husbandry Condemnation of affected parts; possible whole-carcass rejection Inspect live pigs; trim and condemn affected tissue
Skin tears Over-sharp scraper; excessive pressure Reduced shelf life; bacterial entry Use bell scraper; moderate pressure
Dirty skin (grey, smelly) Dirty wash water; poor rinsing Rapid spoilage; food safety risk Potable water; final chlorinated rinse

Source: Compiled from FAO (1991), Guidelines for slaughtering, meat cutting and further processing; and from ILRI, "Smallholder pig production and marketing in Uganda" (2011), ILRI Research Report.

5. Removing Hooves and Lower Legs

Hooves are removed after scalding and singeing, while the carcass is still warm. Use a sharp knife, a meat saw, or a cleaver. The cut is made at the fetlock joint (the joint just above the hoof), not through the middle of the leg bone. Cutting through the bone leaves sharp splinters that can injure workers and contaminate the meat.

In many African markets, hooves and lower legs are a valuable by-product â sold separately for soup, stew, or "paya." Do not discard them. Clean them thoroughly, singe off any remaining hair, and package them for sale. In Nigeria and Ghana, a set of four cleaned pig trotters can fetch 15â25% of the value of the whole carcass. Treat them as a profit centre, not waste.

6. Inspecting the Skin for Wounds or Abscesses

After washing, inspect the entire skin under good light. Look for:

  • Abscesses: Firm, raised, pus-filled swellings, often at injection sites on the neck or rump. These must be trimmed away with a wide margin (at least 2 cm of clean tissue around the abscess) and condemned. Never cut into an abscess over the carcass â it spreads bacteria.
  • Wounds and scars: Open wounds, bite marks, or healed scars. Trim and condemn affected tissue.
  • Skin lesions: Ringworm, mange, or erysipelas lesions. These may indicate a wider disease problem â consult a veterinarian before selling the meat.
  • Bruises: Dark, discoloured areas from rough handling. Trim them off; bruised meat spoils faster.

Record every defect in your slaughter log. Over time, this data tells you which suppliers or transport methods are causing losses, and lets you negotiate price or change practices.

â  SAFETY WARNING â FIRE, HOT WATER, AND SHARP TOOLS

  • Hot water (60â65 Â°C) causes severe burns in seconds. Always wear waterproof gloves, boots, and an apron. Never reach into the scalding tank with bare hands.
  • Blowtorches and open fires are a fire and explosion risk. Keep a fire extinguisher or a bucket of sand and water within reach. Never use a blowtorch near fuel, dry grass, or gas cylinders. Check hoses and connections for leaks before every use.
  • Sharp knives and cleavers cause serious cuts. Use cut-resistant gloves on the non-knife hand. Keep blades sharp â a blunt knife requires more force and slips more easily.
  • Ensure good ventilation. Burning hair and singeing produce smoke and fumes. Work outdoors or in a well-ventilated area. Never singe in an enclosed room.
  • Zoonotic disease risk: Wear gloves and cover any open cuts on your hands. Wash hands and equipment with soap and clean water after handling any carcass.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Heat water to 60â65 Â°C â verify with a thermometer, not by hand.
  2. Immerse the whole pig for 3â5 minutes (adjust by weight) and roll it so all surfaces contact the water.
  3. Scrape the head and ears first, then the body, belly, and legs â use a bell scraper or blunt blade.
  4. Singe with a moving flame (blowtorch or open fire) to remove fine hair; never hold the flame in one spot.
  5. Scrape again after singeing to remove burnt hair and scorched skin.
  6. Wash with clean, potable water â final rinse with 50â100 ppm chlorine if water quality is uncertain.
  7. Remove hooves at the fetlock joint and clean them for separate sale â do not discard.
  8. Inspect the whole skin for abscesses, wounds, and bruises; trim and condemn affected tissue with a wide margin.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Guidelines for slaughtering, meat cutting and further processing (Animal Production and Health Paper 91)
  • FAO â Manual on meat inspection for developing countries (FAO Animal Production and Health Paper 119)
  • ILRI â Smallholder pig production and marketing research (open access publications)
  • WOAH (OIE) â Terrestrial Animal Health Code: Chapter on slaughter of animals
  • Uganda National Bureau of Standards â US EAS 12:2013, Fresh pork â Specification

Prepared for the RISE AFRICA Skills programme â Processing a Pig Fully. This practical reference is intended for small and medium agribusiness operators. Always comply with national meat hygiene regulations and consult a qualified veterinarian or meat inspector where required.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for scalding a pig?
quiz.explanation: Water between 60Â°C and 65Â°C is hot enough to loosen hair but not cook the skin.

quiz.q: How can you test if the water is the right temperature without a thermometer?
options: A) Dip your finger and count to 10
C) Touch the water with your lips
quiz.explanation: The elbow test is a common method: the water should feel very hot but not scalding.

quiz.q: What happens if the scalding water is too hot?
options: A) The hair falls off easily
B) The skin becomes tough and may tear
D) The pig becomes easier to scrape
quiz.explanation: Too hot water cooks the skin, making it tough and prone to tearing during scraping.

quiz.q: Why is wood ash sometimes added to scalding water?
options: A) To make the water hotter
B) To help break down hair and make scraping easier
C) To add flavor to the meat
quiz.explanation: Wood ash contains alkaline substances that help loosen hair and aid in scraping.

quiz.q: How long should a pig typically be immersed in scalding water?
quiz.explanation: The time varies with size and hair thickness, but 2 to 5 minutes is typical.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for scraping hair off a scalded pig?
options: B) A sharp knife or specialized scraper
quiz.explanation: A sharp knife or scraper removes hair efficiently without tearing the skin.

quiz.q: When scraping, in which direction should you move the knife?
options: B) In the direction of hair growth
quiz.explanation: Scraping in the direction of hair growth helps remove hair without cutting the skin.

quiz.q: Why should you work quickly after removing the pig from hot water?
options: A) The pig will get cold
B) The hair becomes harder to remove as the pig cools
C) The skin will change color
quiz.explanation: As the pig cools, the hair sets and becomes more difficult to scrape off.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of singeing after scraping?
options: B) To remove remaining fine hairs and kill bacteria
C) To add color to the skin
D) To make the skin softer
quiz.explanation: Singeing removes fine hairs and helps sanitize the skin.

quiz.q: How far should a blowtorch flame be held from the pig's skin?
quiz.explanation: Holding the flame 15-20 cm away prevents burning the skin while effectively singeing hair.

quiz.q: What should you do if you don't have a blowtorch for singeing?
options: B) Use a fire made with dry grass or wood
quiz.explanation: A fire can be used to singe hair by passing the pig over the flames.

quiz.q: Why is singeing done in a well-ventilated area?
options: A) To keep the fire burning
B) To avoid smoke inhalation and strong odors
C) To prevent the pig from catching fire
D) To make the process faster
quiz.explanation: Burning hair produces smoke and a strong smell, so good ventilation is necessary.

quiz.q: After singeing, what should you do to the blackened skin?
quiz.explanation: The burnt layer should be scraped off to reveal clean skin.

quiz.q: What can be used as an abrasive to help remove burnt hair and dirt?
quiz.explanation: Ash acts as a mild abrasive and helps neutralize odors.

quiz.q: Why might you wash the pig with lime juice or vinegar?
options: B) To remove lingering smell and brighten the skin
C) To make the skin softer
quiz.explanation: Lime juice or vinegar helps remove odors and gives the skin a cleaner appearance.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a wound or abscess on the skin?
options: B) Cut it out and discard
quiz.explanation: Wounds and abscesses should be removed to ensure food safety.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for removing hooves?
options: B) A sharp knife or meat saw
quiz.explanation: A sharp knife or meat saw can cut through the joint and bone cleanly.

quiz.q: Where is the joint for removing the hoof located?
options: A) At the top of the leg
C) In the middle of the leg
quiz.explanation: The joint is just above the hoof, where the leg narrows.

quiz.q: What can you do with the hooves and lower legs if you don't want to discard them?
options: B) Clean and cook them for soups or stews
D) Throw them in the river
quiz.explanation: In many cultures, hooves and lower legs are considered delicacies and can be cooked.

quiz.q: Why is it important to inspect the skin for abscesses?
options: A) To determine the pig's age
B) To ensure the meat is safe to eat
D) To see if the pig is fat
quiz.explanation: Abscesses can indicate infection, and consuming them can cause illness.

quiz.q: What does an abscess feel like under the skin?
quiz.explanation: An abscess is a pocket of pus that feels like a lump under the skin.

quiz.q: If you find many abscesses or signs of serious disease, what should you do?
options: B) Consult a veterinarian or discard the carcass
quiz.explanation: Serious disease may make the meat unsafe; professional advice or disposal is necessary.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of steps after scalding?
options: A) Scrape, singe, wash, remove hooves
B) Singe, scrape, wash, remove hooves
C) Scrape, wash, singe, remove hooves
D) Wash, scrape, singe, remove hooves
quiz.explanation: After scalding, you scrape, then singe, then wash, then remove hooves.

quiz.q: Why is teamwork helpful during scalding and scraping?
options: A) It makes the work faster and easier
B) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Having one person hold the pig, another scrape, and another manage water speeds up the process.

quiz.q: What safety precaution should you take when using a blowtorch?
options: B) Check for leaks and keep away from children
D) Point it at yourself to test
quiz.explanation: Checking for leaks and keeping children away prevents accidents.

quiz.q: What should you do with the water after scalding?
options: B) Dispose of it properly away from water sources
quiz.explanation: Scalding water contains hair and dirt and should be disposed of properly to avoid contamination.

quiz.q: How can you tell if a pig has been properly scalded?
options: A) The hair falls off easily when rubbed
B) The skin is bright red
quiz.explanation: Properly scalded hair loosens and can be rubbed off with minimal effort.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of using water that is too cool for scalding?
options: A) The hair will be hard to remove
quiz.explanation: Cool water does not loosen the hair enough, making scraping difficult.

quiz.q: Why should you keep your scraping knife sharp?
options: B) To remove hair efficiently without tearing the skin
C) To make the job take longer
quiz.explanation: A sharp knife scrapes hair cleanly, while a dull one tears the skin.

quiz.q: What should you do after removing hooves and lower legs?
options: A) Wash the legs with clean water
quiz.explanation: Washing removes dirt and bacteria before further processing.
